This is not a vote on the general principle of assisted dying.

It is a vote on a specific Bill, and this one gets it dangerously wrong.

️ There is nothing in this Bill to prevent people from starving themselves to become eligible, and amendments to fix that aren’t even being considered
️ It removes judicial oversight and replaces it with a panel that lacks independence

Under its current wording:

️ People with anorexia, a treatable mental illness, could be eligible
️ People with chronic but manageable conditions, like diabetes, have accessed assisted dying abroad

But compassion must be matched by care, safety, and strong legal safeguards. And this Bill is not safe.

It contains serious loopholes, ones that experts and over 50 charities have warned us about.

8/  Economists Weber and Krebs argue: “Price controls should be part of the policy toolbox to respond to shocks to systemically important sectors…”
7/  Brazil froze prices on staple foods like rice and beans during economic shocks  The UK trialled voluntary price caps on basics like bread and milk in 2023 to ease pressure at the checkout
6/  France capped electricity bills to help people manage rising costs  Spain cut energy taxes and introduced rent caps to ease pressure Both governments stepped in to protect people from inflation
5/ Everyone deserves access to life’s essentials. If prices climb and government doesn’t act, more people will fall behind.
4/ When energy costs rise, so do prices for food, transport, and housing. These increases affect daily life across the board.
3. Fuel, heating, and electricity could soon become more expensive. Even with price caps in place, many of us are still paying more than we can afford.
2/ The UK doesn’t import much fuel from the region, but global markets still shape what we pay. When prices rise abroad, we feel it here too

To win the next election and show that democracy delivers, we need to get living standards rising.

That means pulling these three levers.

This means to reduce poverty, we need to increase the payments which make up 40% of their incomes.

And lower poverty means less pressure on public services, and increased future productivity. It’s an investment with a long-term growth payoff.

But, those at the bottom are not affected that much by wage increases. 

Universal Credit is an in-work benefit. Wage increases reduce eligibility, meaning for every £1 increase in the minimum wage, the poorest only keep 17p.

Getting wages rising helps all, and it helps the (squeezed) middle by the most.

To get wages rising this, we need to get growth rising (including from interest rate cuts), increase public sector wages, and boost bargaining power of workers.

We also need to increase incomes.

But where do people get their incomes from?

For those at the bottom, it’s wages and social security. For those in the middle, it’s entirely wages. For those at the top, it’s wages and wealth payments.

This means investing in clean energy, that is up to 75% cheaper than gas, while insulating homes and finding innovative ways to reduce tariffs. 

It means building more homes, including social homes. 

It means capping the cost of childcare.

Getting costs down helps everyone, but especially poorer households.

The poorest spend almost half of their income on housing and energy alone. 

Cutting the UK’s huge energy, housing, and childcare costs down will make a big difference.

Making people better off is how we win the next election.

There are three ‘levers’ we can pull to do this: costs, wages & social security payments.

We need to pull all three.

3/ Leaks are draining our future.

Our crumbling infrastructure is losing 3 billion litres of water daily, 20% of the supply.

Ofwat set a target to halve leakage by 2050. But in 2023, over half of firms missed their own targets. In fact, most saw an increase in annual leakage.

2/ For-profit companies can't be trusted with vital infrastructure.

During 35 years of privatised water, no new reservoirs have been built. Worse, 25 have been sold off.

Andrew Sells, ex-Chair of Natural England, says water companies are putting profits before water resilience.

1/ This is what we're up against: the Environment Agency warns parts of England could run out of water by 2050.

We're already at five-to-midnight on the water doomsday clock.

We must build resilience into our water system or face the unthinkable: taps running dry.

 Bring your dog inside into a shady, well ventilated, cool room

Call your local vets and follow their instructions

Cool them down by pouring cool to water on them

Do not leave animals in hot cars

 Ensure they aren't locked in rooms with no ventilation

 Provide access to plenty of cool, clean water

Do not exercise in the heat

 Less hassle

 You own your home outright, no lease ticking down

7️⃣ Next steps: The government will lay regulations in Parliament to finalise the law.

A significant breakthrough in tackling the most hazardous and life-threatening conditions in social housing.

6️⃣ Why does this matter?

Too many social housing tenants live in unfit conditions with little power to demand change. This law forces landlords to take responsibility.

5️⃣ The government is also introducing wider reforms to social housing standards.

Plans include a new Decent Homes Standard, mandatory electrical safety checks, and stronger accountability for landlords.

4️⃣ By 2027, Awaab’s Law will apply to all major housing hazards except overcrowding.

This phased approach ensures the most urgent dangers are tackled first, while full protections are introduced over time.

3️⃣ In 2026, the law will expand to cover excess cold, fire risks, falls, and hygiene hazards.

Unsafe housing isn’t just about damp - freezing homes, electrical faults, and dangerous structures also put tenants’ lives at risk.

2️⃣ All emergency repairs, regardless of the issue, must be completed within 24 hours.

Tenants have long faced unacceptable delays in urgent repairs. This requirement forces landlords to act immediately on serious hazards.

1️⃣ From October 2025, social landlords must fix damp and mould hazards within set timescales.

Damp and mould are serious health risks, linked to respiratory conditions and, in extreme cases, tragedies like the death of Awaab Ishak.

Our Labour government has confirmed it will bring Awaab’s Law into force for the social rented sector from October 2025. 

This is a major step in tackling unsafe housing in Peckham.

This definition of HBA, drafted by barrister Naomi Wiseman, has been endorsed by victims and the VAWG sector.

Writing it into law will provide clarity across sectors, ensuring consistent identification, response and recording of HBA, and leading to better protection for victims.

- HBA is misunderstood or overlooked by professionals and legal bodies

- HBA is inconsistently identified due to competing definitions

- The role of multiple perpetrators is missed

- Data collection is poor

- And, ultimately, the human cost will continue to grow.

Failing to address it specifically means:

Fawziyah’s abuse was characterised by key elements of HBA:

- Collective perpetration

- Honour-driven motivations

- Control and punishment

- Shame as a barrier to leave

Had her case been recognised for the complex abuse it involved, Fawziyah might have had a chance to escape.

Her story, told through the C4 documentary ‘The Push: Murder on the Cliff’, highlights systemic failures to recognise the abuse she faced and take suitable action.

(19/19) I am absolutely determined to continue to fight for better health outcomes for people in Plymouth, and whilst I am over the moon about last week’s news at Derriford, this victory only makes me even more determined to go on and get more for our city and its people.

(18/19) This win will make an enormous difference for staff and patients, but I know it is not the final piece of the puzzle. We still need improvements in healthcare settings right across the city, at Derriford, at GP surgeries and in dentistry.
(17/19) This will house an Urgent Treatment Centre, not to be confused with the new A&E which will be party of the main hospital building. I am deeply impressed by hospital staff at every level.
(16/19) The team at Derriford have almost completed the new Dartmoor Building which has sprung up overlooking Derriford Roundabout.
(15/19) This is incredibly exciting news for Plymouth, and as a city we should feel incredibly proud that we have secured such immense investment into our hospital.
(14/19) And now here we are, at the start of 2025, with confirmation from the Health Secretary that the new A&E will be built, and that the work will start within the next 12 months.
(13/19) He met staff, heard first-hand about the many challenges they face, and was told what a new A&E Department would mean to them and folk across Plymouth.

(12/19) It was then that I knew the most compelling way to make our case to the Health Secretary would be for him to visit himself and meet some of the incredible staff. So, I invited him and over Christmas he made a quiet, low-key visit to Derriford Hospital.

(11/19) At the start of December I was invited to join staff on a night shift at Derriford, and given the opportunity to see the amazing work that they do under such difficult circumstances. I saw heroics that night, but I know that it is simply what happens there every day.

(10/19) I was doing all I could to make sure that decision makers in Whitehall understood how important this project was for our city. But ultimately, it was hard to know whether the message was getting through.

(9/19) Behind the scenes I was meeting with the Health Secretary, making our case for a new A&E and liaising with Derriford’s senior leadership to make sure the message I was sending to government was the correct one.
(8/19) I wrote to Boris Johnson calling out his lies, asking him to apologise to the people of Plymouth and I asked a question to the Deputy PM during PMQs, securing a meeting with ministers.
(7/19) So, the government had to assess whether all of these projects, including Derriford, were viable and affordable. That’s when my campaign really stepped up a gear.

(6/19) Then, when the Labour Party came into power last year, we discovered that the Conservatives had not allocated funding to the project or the 40 other promised projects across the country. It had always been an empty promise in an attempt to win votes.

(5/19) We were first promised a "New Hospital" in 2019. It then turned out that it wasn’t a new hospital at all, it was a new – and still very much needed - A&E department. We were then promised this new A&E year after year, but it never came.
(4/19) We had to work hard to secure this essential investment in our city because of the empty promises made by Boris Johnson and his former Tory MP here in Plymouth.
(3/19) This announcement has come after a relentless campaign from myself and the Labour Party here in Plymouth. But we never should have needed a campaign in the first place.

(2/19) Last week it was finally announced that we would be getting that new A&E. It’s incredible news for Plymouth, and I want to take an opportunity to reflect on my campaign, and how we got here, and what comes next.

7/7

There are many kinds of breast cancer and not all treatments are for all breast cancers. My cancer is triple negative so will not respond to hormonal treatments. How anyone responds to treatment depends on type of cancer and their own unique genetic set up. My cancer is as unique as I am. 

6/7

I have an incurable cancer but that doesn’t mean I’m about to die or that I am feeling poorly. My treatment has made my cancer stable for now. I will work and play as I always did.

5/7

Treatments can control but not cure the cancer. 

My recent treatment was surgery. That has controlled it for now. I will probably need other treatments in the future as and when the cancer becomes detectable again.

4/7

No evidence of disease or active disease (NED or NEAD) does not mean cured. It means right now imaging and testing shows either no detectable cancers or the cancers there are aren’t currently growing.

3/7

I cannot “beat this”. 
There is no cure for metastatic breast cancer. It’s also known as advanced, secondary or stage 4. The only way I beat it is by dying of something else first.

Renters have been getting a raw deal for too long.

The Renters' Rights Bill is a golden opportunity to fix our broken rental system.

The government must pursue every available measure to protect renters from rising costs, disrepair, unfair evictions and unscrupulous landlords.

Another vital lever in this regard could be creating a new right for tenants to withhold rent when repairs aren't carried out within appropriate timescales – as proposed by my friend @zarahsultana.bsky.social.
The new enforcement powers in today's Bill are also welcome but it’s also essential that the government ensures local authorities have the funding and resources they need to use them.

I also support @rentersreformco.bsky.social in their call for a National Rental Affordability Commission, to explore other options to bring down rents relative to incomes -including the implementation of rent controls (in partnership with regional mayors).

I’m pleased to be supporting @paulabarkermp.bsky.social's amendment to better protect tenants from unaffordable rent increases.

Instead of capping rent rises in line with speculative market prices, this amendment would cap them in line with wages or inflation - whichever is lowest.

Renting a one-bed home in Lambeth already costs the average person more than half of their take-home pay.

As renters' unions have been pointing out, in the current economic climate, a large rent hike is just a no fault eviction by another name.

But if this landmark Bill is going to truly reform the rental sector and shift the balance of power to create a more equal relationship between renters and landlords, then more must be done, particularly in terms of rental costs.

These are all vital steps, which go some way towards protecting renters from the most unscrupulous landlords, providing more secure tenure, and driving up living standards in the private rental sector.

New measures to strengthen enforcement action against slum private landlords are also very welcome: extending the Decent Homes Standard to the private rental sector and widening council enforcement powers (as well as the financial penalties available to fund this).

The Bill also includes provisions that focus on affordability, ensuring that: rent increases can no longer be written into contracts, landlords can only legally increase rents once a year (and only in line with “market rates”) and tenants are protected from egregious rent hikes.

The Renters’ Rights Bill will finally scrap Section 21 no fault evictions, which let landlords evict tenants without providing a reason.

Nearly 1,000,000 people were evicted under these laws in the last Parliament alone, adding to the homelessness crisis facing our country.

Private renters have faced eyewatering rent hikes in recent years for homes with the highest disrepair levels of any type of housing tenure. 

The ease with which renters can be evicted has made it harder for tenants to challenge landlords on these issues.

The Renters’ Rights Bill is back before Parliament today.

This long overdue legislation contains new measures that will provide renters with basic security and place some basic responsibility on landlords.

I’ll be voting for several amendments to strengthen it.

It falls again to Labour to tackle unacceptably long NHS waits - I look forward to the new NHS plan outlining further steps to tackle progress tackling waits in all sectors of the NHS.

Welcome steps here include properly embedding ‘advice and guidance’, allowing GPs to consult hospital specialists without a referral, and extending community diagnostic capacity. 

These reforms are more convenient for patients - while also increasing productivity & lowering waiting times for all.

As well as measures to get through the backlog of the existing waiting list, the government is also wisely focused on ensuring new referrals to secondary care are right. 

Specialist teams spend too much of their time seeing newly referred patients before necessary diagnostics are available.

This is particularly crucial in Orthopaedics - a specialty with some of the longest waiting times.

So the Govt’s plan to expand the number of Surgical Hubs offering ring-fenced elective capacity is critical - as are wider plans to improve social care & reduce emergency bed demand and thus boarding.

Effective separation of elective bed capacity from 'boarded' overspill emergency patients is critical for maximising volume, making sure that surgical teams' time is efficiently used, and getting *all* patients cared for on the right ward for them.

There’s a simple way to allay that scepticism though. The Cabinet Office just needs to tell us when they received the claims for the expenses Boris Johnson incurred in 2022/23, and when they decided to let him have the money. Watch this space for the answers. (8/8)

But that surely can’t be right. Otherwise that would have to mean Alex Burghart wasn’t being entirely factual in the PQ answer he gave me in April 2023, and that the Cabinet Office were also mistaken when they published their annual report in September 2023. (7/8)

Now, you might think it’s no accident that the Cabinet Office happened to weaken the rules preventing late payments in the very year when Boris Johnson realised he was going to be £68k out of pocket for failing to get his expense claims in on time. (6/8)

So far, so clear. But then we get to the Cabinet Office annual report for 2023-24, published yesterday, which tells us that Boris Johnson DID submit a late claim for £67,803 of office expenses incurred during the 2022-23 financial year, and was reimbursed in full. (5/8)

That seemed pretty definitive from Alex Burghart, and when the 2022-23 Annual Report he had mentioned in his answer was published five months later, it was equally definitive that no claims had been received – late or otherwise – from Boris Johnson. (4/8)

That got me interested. Why had they changed the guidance to make the rules less explicit about when claims needed to be submitted, and whether late claims would be accepted? So I asked the Cabinet Office whether any late claims had come in that year just gone? (3/8)

So yes, the PM needed a reset. But it also needed an additional mission – a National Adaptation Plan to safeguard our food security, better prepare the country for a future of more extreme weather and put nature at the heart of our response to climate change.

Nor should we ignore the impact extreme temperatures have on our food security. The Climate Change Committee warned five years ago that more frequent weather extremes would damage crops and livestock, making food prices more volatile.

But it’s not just flooding – we’ve also seen extreme heat in the last few years. Does anyone really believe our transport infrastructure is ready for summer heatwaves? Can our homes cope with this extreme heat? On all of this government is silent let alone prioritising it.

We need to go further faster. But it needs to be joined up. Building more homes, especially social, is essential. But building on floodplains not only condemns future owners to the misery of likely flooding, it also stops the land from absorbing and holding back floodwater.

The UK is falling far short of what’s needed. The adaptation plans lack the pace and ambition to address the climate risks which are happening now. Fewer than half of the short-term actions needed to address the most urgent risks are in progress.

Back here in the UK we need to sit up and take note. The government’s advisers, the Climate Change Committee, issued a review of the National Adaptation Programme earlier this year and it was scathing.
The cost of this is eye-watering. The Valencia region has asked for over 30 billion Euros in relief and the insurance costs are expected to run to several billion more.

Even if we limit global heating to 1.5C, and that looks more and more unlikely, significant changes to the climate and our weather systems are already baked in. This means more extreme weather like the storms we saw a few weeks ago.

A lot could be said about today’s 'new milestones'. But there has been little focus on one major omission: the UK has no credible plan for how we will cope with extreme changes in the climate. 

That’s why I’m calling for an extra mission: a National Adaptation Plan

It is now the duty of the whole house to ensure that the Bill is in the strongest position – addressing as many of the concerns people have expressed as possible – before being brought back for its final vote.

It was an extremely difficult decision, but it is for those reasons that I voted against.

Next steps

The Bill has passed its second reading. It is now time for Parliament to scrutinise and debate the details before bringing it to a final vote.
Many of my MP colleagues eloquently set out these concerns in the debate yesterday, including the particular risk to those from minority groups.

Whilst many people shared fears about coercion, I was particularly concerned about people – many of whom already vulnerable by reason of their illness and care needs - feeling a duty to die. People who might be worried that they are burdening their family or society and opting to get out of the way.

I believe that getting this wrong would have incredibly serious consequences, and the risk of getting it wrong with a broken NHS is too high. These are not conditions anyone would wish for our NHS – nor are they conditions I believe anyone would choose to be the landing strip for assisted dying.

Vote

In principle, I support assisted dying. I want people to have dignity at the end of their lives and, with strong safeguards, a say in how they die. But yesterday, I found myself unable to vote for this bill.
Some of the stories I read will stay with me for a very long time.

Many people shared their views and experiences with me. Those letters and emails, calls and meetings, public discussions and social media posts, moved me and helped me decide how to vote. I will be forever grateful for the generosity, bravery and thoughtfulness of those contributions.

This was a difficult, finely balanced decision. Ahead of it, I recognised the duty I owed to my constituents – as well as to myself and the wider country – to read widely, engage extensively and think deeply until the last moment. To be as informed as possible when reaching a final position.
